title: Characterization of piezoelectric MEMS vibration energy harvesters using random vibration

sections.heading: Characterization of piezoelectric MEMS vibration energy harvesters using random vibration
sections.text:
Shuichi Murakami1\*, Takeshi Yoshimura2, Yusuke Kanaoka1, Kazuki Tsuda1, Kazuo Satoh1, Kensuke Kanda3, and Norifumi Fujimura2

1Osaka Research Institute of Industrial Science and Technology, Izumi, Osaka 594-1157, Japan   
2Osaka Prefecture University, Sakai 599-8531, Japan   
3University of Hyogo, Himeji, Hyogo 671-2280, Japan

\*E-mail: sh-murakami@tri-osaka.jp

Received June 7, 2018; accepted August 2, 2018; published online October 11, 2018

In this study, we fabricated piezoelectric MEMS cantilever-type vibration energy harvesters employing ${ \mathsf { P b } } ( Z { \mathsf { r } } , { \mathsf { T i } } ) { \mathsf { O } } _ { 3 }$ films, which were designed to exhibit a resonant frequency of around $1 8 5 \mathsf { H z }$ . The output power was investigated under random vibration whose power spectral density (PSD) was constant in the frequency regime between 150 and $2 2 0 { \mathsf { H z } }$ . The PSD of the output power shows that the cantilever vibrates at the resonant frequency of around $1 8 3 \mathsf { H z }$ , and that the resonant frequency decreases and the full-width at half maximum increases with increasing vibrational acceleration. In comparison with the measurement results under sinusoidal vibration, it was clarified that this phenomenon is caused by the soft spring effect due to the nonlinearity of the cantilever vibration. The power generation under random vibration is proportional to the square of the acceleration not only in the linear region but also in the nonlinear region. $\circledcirc$ 2018 The Japan Society of Applied Physics

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
In recent years, considerable attention has been directed toward energy harvesters. This is because energy harvesters generate electrical energy from environmental energy, which is usually discarded but could be an energy source for powering microdevices, such as small wireless sensor nodes in a sensing network, structural health monitoring systems, biomedical implants, and environmental condition monitoring systems. Energy harvesting is one of the key technologies for realizing the Internet of Things (IoT) and the Trillion Sensors Universe.

For the power source of the energy harvesters, light, thermal gradients, vibration, and electromagnetic radiation are promising candidates. Among these power sources, none of them are absolutely superior. We can select the power source on the basis of the application, installation place, and so forth. In our study, we have developed vibration energy– harvesters that can convert kinetic energy from vibration into electrical energy, because vibration energy is the most ubiquitous and accessible.1 3) Several transduction methods can be used for energy harvesters including electromagnetic induction, electrostatic induction, anti-magneto restriction effect, and piezoelectricity. Research and development activities are actively conducted for each method. The choice of the transduction method depends mainly on the application since each method has advantages and disadvantages.

Among these methods, piezoelectricity has received much attention owing to the direct conversion of vibration energy into electrical energy with a high power density and the simplicity of its device structure. Furthermore, energy– harvesters based on piezoelectricity are suitable for miniaturization and easy to integrate since they are highly compatible with the MEMS process.3 6) Therefore, we have focused on piezoelectric MEMS vibration energy harvesters using MEMS technology. Although $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { Z r } , \mathrm { T i } ) { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ (PZT) is widely accepted as the electromechanical transducer material,6 14) we have proposed that the lead-free ${ \mathrm { B i F e O } } _ { 3 }$ piezoelectric film is a promising candidate for the piezoelectric energy harvester, because ${ \mathrm { B i F e O } } _ { 3 }$ has a high figure of merit (FOM) among the ferroelectrics.15 21) We have also demonstrated that MEMS cantilever-type energy harvesters using (100)-oriented ${ \mathrm { B i F e O } } _ { 3 }$ films show the normalized output power of $0 . 9 \mu \mathrm { W } { \cdot } \mathrm { G } ^ { - 2 } { \cdot } \mathrm { m m } ^ { - 2 }$ , which exceeds or is comparable to the best-performing piezoelectric energy harvesters using other piezoelectric films, such as PZT, $( \mathrm { K } , \mathrm { N a } ) \mathrm { N b } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ (KNN), and AlN.19,22 25)

We have also observed the hard spring effect due to the nonlinearity of the cantilever vibration in the measurement results under sinusoidal vibration. When the vibrational frequency ramps up and down around a resonant frequency, the hysteresis is observed in the frequency dependence of output voltage. Furthermore, the resonant frequency increases and the full-width at half maximum (FWHM) increases as the vibrational acceleration increases.19,22 24) Similar measurement results have been reported so far. For instance, Minh have also reported that the energy harvester fabricated employing the KNN piezoelectric film shows the hard spring effect owing to the nonlinearity of the beam deflection and that the bandwidth of the harvester can be increased by the hard or soft spring effect.25) In general, piezoelectric vibration energy harvesters have a high $Q$ -value and a small FWHM (bandwidth). It can be said that increasing the bandwidth is effective in increasing the power generation because the external environmental vibration is broadly distributed in the frequency domain. However, to the best of our knowledge, there have been few reports on the nonlinear characteristics of the power generation and the increase in the bandwidth under random vibration, which is distributed in the wide frequency domain.

In this study, we fabricated typical piezoelectric MEMS cantilever-type vibrational energy harvesters employing PZT films. The power spectral density (PSD) of the output voltage was investigated at various accelerations under random vibration. In comparison with the measurement results using sinusoidal vibration, the nonlinear behavior of the power generation was considered.

sections.heading: 2. Fabrication and experiment
sections.text:
Figure 1(a) shows a schematic structure and a photograph of the fabricated piezoelectric MEMS cantilever-type vibration energy harvesters. It consists of a single cantilever structure, which is composed of a supporting silicon layer, a $\mathrm { P t / T i }$ bottom electrode, a PZT piezoelectric film, a $\mathrm { P t / T i }$ upper electrode, and a proof mass on the tip of the cantilever. A schematic of the MEMS fabrication process of the harvesters is shown in Fig. 1(b). The starting material was a silicon-oninsulator (SOI) wafer with a $2 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick Si device layer, a $1 { \cdot } | | \mathbf { m }$ -thick $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ layer (insulating layer), and a ${ 5 0 0 } \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick Si-bulk layer. The energy harvesters were fabricated as follows:

![](images/5e4f8b0bdd82dadddea60314f215f7d2762d7170dfd47319d42a5147eb9b5cd5.jpg)  
Fig. 1. (Color online) (a) Schematic illustration, photograph, and (b) MEMS fabrication of the cantilever-type piezoelectric energy harvester fabricated employing PZT film.

1) An SOI wafer was oxidized on both sides with a thickness of $1 \mu \mathrm { m }$ .   
2) We used a $\mathrm { P t / T i }$ film as a bottom electrode. The thicknesses of $\mathrm { P t }$ and Ti were 100 and $1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , respectively. The $\mathrm { P t / T i }$ film was deposited on the front surface by sputtering. Subsequently, a PZT piezoelectric film with a thickness of $3 . 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ was prepared by sputtering.   
3) The $\mathrm { P t / T i }$ film was deposited as an upper electrode with a thickness of $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m } / 1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . Then, we patterned the $\mathrm { P t / T i }$ upper electrode, PZT piezoelectric film, and $\mathrm { P t / T i }$ bottom electrode by inductive coupled plasma-reactive ion etching (ICP-RIE), one by one.   
4) An interlayer insulating film $\mathrm { ( T E O S  – S i O _ { 2 } ) }$ ) with a thickness of $0 . 6 \mu \mathrm { m }$ was deposited by CVD and patterned by ICP-RIE.   
5) $\mathrm { P t / T i }$ was deposited by sputtering and patterned by ICP-RIE in order to form electrodes and wires.   
6) To form the cantilevers, we removed the thermally oxidized $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ layer, Si layer and $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ insulating layer on the front surface around the cantilevers. The $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ and Si layers were etched by ICP-RIE and deep RIE, respectively.   
7) The Si-bulk was etched from the back surface by deep RIE to form the cantilever and a proof mass.

We finally fabricated the piezoelectric cantilever-type vibration energy harvesters with a unimorph structure, as shown in Fig. 1(a). The cantilever with the proof mass was designed to exhibit the resonant frequency of around $1 8 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . The width, length, and thickness of the cantilever were $1 \mathrm { m m }$ , $6 \mathrm { m m }$ , and $2 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , respectively. The proof mass was made of the Si-bulk and had dimensions of $3 \times 1 \times 0 . 5 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ , whose weight was $3 . 5 \mathrm { m g }$ . The fabricated harvester was wirebonded on the metal carrier for characterization.

![](images/0251b804b364818a5160afa35ac79985607ed4a6717013a669f3dcc55cf0ddc1.jpg)  
Fig. 2. (Color online) (a) Experimental setup for evaluating the performance of the energy harvester under random vibration. (b) Power spectral density of the acceleration and transient acceleration at the acceleration of $1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) under random vibration.

The experimental setup with a shaker for measuring the output voltage and electrical power of the fabricated energy harvester under random vibration is shown in Fig. 2(a). The random vibrations were generated by a commercial vibration simulator (IMV K2 Sprint) and applied to the harvester in the perpendicular direction using a shaker (IMV PET-05). In this study, we used the random vibration whose PSD of acceleration was constant in the frequency regime between 150 and $2 2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Figure 2(b) shows the PSD and transient acceleration at the acceleration of $1 . 0 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS). A load resistance was connected to the bottom and upper electrodes. By using the vibration simulator, the output voltage across the load resistance was measured, and consequently, the PSD of the output voltage was obtained.

![](images/6ead756924c95cbf3af584d8293abb6280046905311b919445fa6d6dbe09233e.jpg)  
Fig. 3. (Color online) Frequency characteristics of the output voltage at various accelerations ranging from $0 . 0 7 1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) to $4 . 7 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) at the impedance-matched load resistance of $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ under sinusoidal vibration.

![](images/09e8a7b2da81e02f5068b6cb48ae2828e11418ace0cc5206a7cc0a0c9d7bda68.jpg)  
Fig. 4. (Color online) Generation power as a function of acceleration at the resonant frequency and optimal load resistance of $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ under sinusoidal vibration.

We also measured the output voltage across the load resistance under sinusoidal vibration using a lock-in amplifier (NF LI-5640). The sinusoidal vibration was generated by the vibration simulator (IMV K2 Sprint), and the frequency was ramped up and down around the resonant frequency of the harvester at a rate of $0 . 0 1 \mathrm { H z } / \mathrm { s }$ .

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
Figure 3 shows the frequency dependence of output voltage across the impedance-matched load resistance, $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , when the sinusoidal vibration is applied. In this figure, the resonant frequency decreases and FWHM increases, and the resonant curves become more asymmetric with increasing vibrational acceleration. In this study, we define the linear region when the resonant frequency remains constant and the resonant curve is symmetric in the frequency dependence of the output voltage. Moreover, the theoretical maximum power generation is proportional to the square of the vibrational acceleration in the linear region.19) Figure 4 shows the acceleration dependence of power generation at the resonant frequency under sinusoidal vibration. The power generation was determined by dividing the square of the output voltage at the resonant frequency by the load resistance. The power generation was proportional to the square of the vibrational acceleration in the acceleration region $[ < 1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS)], but not proportional in the acceleration region $[ > 1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS)].

![](images/21122ea1c423ba609811f39dfab7b6f8bf42571a717dc263106750f4b495141d.jpg)  
Fig. 5. (Color online) Displacement of the tip of the cantilever under random vibration at the acceleration of $2 3 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) and the optimal load resistance of $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .

According to Figs. 3 and 4, the acceleration region $[ < 1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS)] is the linear region, whereas the other region $[ > 1$ $\mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS)] is the nonlinear region. These phenomena imply that the soft spring effect due to the nonlinearity of the cantilever vibration becomes remarkable, and the resonant frequency decreases as the vibrational acceleration increases. The soft spring effect is attributed to the decrease in the stiffness and apparent spring constant under the largedeflection condition of the cantilever.26)

The normalized power generation was $3 . 3 \mu \mathrm { W } { \cdot } \mathrm { G } ^ { - 2 } { \cdot } \mathrm { m m } ^ { - 2 }$ $( \mathrm { G } = 9 . 8 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 } )$ ) at the resonant frequency of around $1 8 3 \mathrm { H z }$ in the linear region. The mechanical quality factor $( Q _ { \mathrm { m } } )$ was 408, which was determined from the measurement under the short-circuit mode. In this study, the measurement under the short-circuit mode was performed at the sufficiently low acceleration of $0 . 0 7 1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) and load resistance of $2 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . We also determined the electromechanical coupling factor $( K ^ { 2 } )$ to be $0 . 1 9 \%$ , which is experimentally calculated using the following equation:27)

$$
K ^ { 2 } = \frac { f _ { \mathrm { O C } } ^ { 2 } - f _ { \mathrm { S C } } ^ { 2 } } { f _ { \mathrm { S C } } ^ { 2 } } ,
$$

where $f _ { \mathrm { O C } } ^ { 2 }$ and $f _ { \mathrm { S C } } ^ { 2 }$ are the resonant frequencies under the measurements in the open-circuit mode $( R _ { \mathrm { L } } = 5 \mathbf { M } \Omega )$ and short-circuit mode $( R _ { \mathrm { L } } = 2 \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ at the sufficiently low acceleration of $0 . 0 7 1 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) in the linear region, respectively. These power generation characteristics of the energy harvester, which was fabricated in this study, are typical among the energy harvesters fabricated using the PZT piezoelectric films.

We have measured the power generation characteristics using random vibration. Figure 5 shows the displacement of the tip of the cantilever under random vibration, whose PSD of acceleration was constant in the frequency regime between 150 and $2 2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , and the vibration acceleration and load resistance were $2 3 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) and $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , respectively. In this figure, the cantilever vibrates at the frequency of around $1 8 3 \mathrm { H z }$ , which is almost the same as the resonant frequency under sinusoidal vibration.

Furthermore, we varied the acceleration from $0 . 2 3 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) to $2 3 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) and obtained the PSD of output voltage by using the vibration simulator as shown in Fig. 6. The resonant frequency is around $1 8 3 \mathrm { H z }$ , which is almost the same as the resonant frequency under sinusoidal vibration. It is also shown that the PSD curves become more asymmetric and that the resonant frequency decreases; conversely, FWHM increases with increasing vibrational acceleration.

![](images/eb2322905949459d181ee59be047bba099888f5e8cbb2d30ed132c23700dda8d.jpg)  
Fig. 6. (Color online) Power spectral density of the output voltage of the fabricated energy harvester at various accelerations from $0 . 2 3 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) to $2 3 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS) at the optimal load resistance of $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .

![](images/da2a4f62df22f7c66292739d094cf31e61434a5dce7a07a9d5a642530ff542d2.jpg)  
Fig. 7. (Color online) Acceleration dependences of resonant frequency (blue circles) and FWHM (red circles), which were determined from the power spectral density of the output voltage at the optimal load resistance of $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ under random vibration.

Therefore, we estimated the resonant frequency and FWHM as functions of acceleration, as shown in Fig. 7. The resonant frequency decreases, and conversely, FWHM increases remarkably when the vibrational acceleration exceeds $3 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS), which is the nonlinear region. On the other hand, the PSD curves are symmetric and the resonant frequencies are constant when the vibrational acceleration is lower than $3 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS), which is the linear region. We have obtained similar measurement results under sinusoidal vibration. Thus, it is concluded that the characterization under random vibration is also affected significantly by the nonlinearity behavior such as the soft spring effect.

Figure 8 shows the acceleration dependence of the power generation of the fabricated PZT piezoelectric energy harvester. The blue circles show the measurement results under the random vibration, which were determined by integrating the PSD in Fig. 6 by the frequency and dividing by the impedance-matched load resistance of $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . In Fig. 8, the power generation under random vibration is proportional to the square of the acceleration not only in the linear region but also in the nonlinear region. The red circles show the power generation estimated from the measurement result under sinusoidal vibration. To compare the measurement results under the random and sinusoidal vibrations, the power generation $( P )$ shown by the red circles in Fig. 8 was determined using the following equation:

![](images/5fb89b1bf3b57b733dec7dc14d2fc389e4e500f24656679f15f2d4ee0aea6760.jpg)  
Fig. 8. (Color online) Acceleration characteristics of the power generation at a load resistance of $1 8 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . The blue circles show the power generations determined from the power spectral density under random vibration in Fig. 6. The red circles show the power generation estimated from the output voltage as a function of frequency under sinusoidal vibration in Fig. 3 in the case of applying random vibration using Eq. (2).

$$
P = \sum _ { i } \frac { V ^ { 2 } ( f _ { i } ) } { R _ { \mathrm { L } } } \frac { 1 } { N } \frac { \Delta f _ { \mathrm { s i n e } } } { \Delta f _ { \mathrm { r a n d o m } } } ,
$$

where $V ( f _ { i } )$ is the output voltage, which was measured at $0 . 0 1 \mathrm { H z }$ intervals in the frequency regime between 180 and $1 8 6 \mathrm { H z }$ , $N$ is the number of measurement points, and $\Delta f _ { \mathrm { s i n e } }$ and $\Delta f _ { \mathrm { r a n d o m } }$ are the frequency regime widths of the sinusoidal and random vibrations, respectively. In this equation, we summed up the square of each output voltage shown in Fig. 3, divided it by the load resistance and the number of measurement points, and multiplied it by the ratio of the frequency regime width of the random and sinusoidal vibrations to make the applied vibration energy the same. The ratio $( \Delta f _ { \mathrm { s i n e } } / \Delta f _ { \mathrm { r a n d o m } } )$ was calculated to be $6 / 7 0 [ = ( 1 8 6 - 1 8 0 ) / ( 2 2 0 - 1 5 0 ) ]$ since the PSD of the random vibration is constant in the frequency regime between 150 and $2 2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ .

In Fig. 8, the estimated power generation (red circles) is proportional to the square of the acceleration, and almost the same as those measured under random vibration (blue circles) in the linear region. It was confirmed that the applied vibration energy matched between the random and sinusoidal vibrations. Therefore, we can predict the power generation under random vibration from the characteristics under sinusoidal vibration in the linear region. On the other hand, the power generation estimated from the results under sinusoidal vibration tends to deviate from the square of the acceleration in the nonlinear region. It is under consideration why this difference occurs in the nonlinear region from the viewpoint of the nonlinearity behavior such as the soft spring effect and air damping.

The bandwidth of the piezoelectric MEMS cantilever-type vibrational energy harvesters could be increased by the soft or hard spring effect.25) In general, increasing the bandwidth is important for generating the output power efficiently since the environmental vibration is distributed in the broad frequency domain. The power generation under random vibration is proportional to the square of the acceleration also in the nonlinear region. This might be due to the increase in the bandwidth because of the soft spring effect. The details of the power generation mechanism are under consideration by using the mass-spring-damper system model.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text: We fabricated a piezoelectric MEMS cantilever-type vibration energy harvester using a PZT film, which was designed to exhibit a resonant frequency of around $1 8 5 \mathrm { H z }$ . We performed measurements using sinusoidal vibration. From the frequency dependence of the output voltage at the impedance-matched load resistance, the resonant frequency decreases and FWHM increases with increasing acceleration. Furthermore, the resonant curves become more asymmetric. These phenomena are attributed to the soft spring effect due to the nonlinearity of the cantilever deflection. The normalized power generation was determined to be 3.3 $\mu \mathrm { W } { \cdot } \mathrm { G } ^ { - 2 } { \cdot } \mathrm { m m } ^ { - 2 }$ at the resonant frequency of around $1 8 3 \mathrm { H z }$ in the linear region, which is typical among the PZT piezoelectric MEMS vibration energy harvesters. We examined the characteristics under random vibration, whose PSD of the acceleration was constant in the frequency regime between 150 and $2 2 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . The resonant frequency decreases and FWHM increases when the acceleration is higher than $3 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ (RMS), which implies that the characteristics under random vibration are also affected by the nonlinearity behavior similar to those under sinusoidal vibration. The power generation under random vibration is proportional to the square of the acceleration not only in the linear region but also in the nonlinear region, and agreed with the power generation estimated from the frequency dependence of the output voltage under sinusoidal vibration only in the linear region.
